title: First-Order ODEs

blocks.x: A differential equation (DE) is an equation that contains a function and its derivatives. If the function depends on one variable only, the equation is an ordinary differential equation (ODE). If it depends on two or more variables, the equation is a partial differential equation (PDE). We start with ODEs.
The order of an ODE is the highest derivative in it. The equation $y' + 2y = x$ is first order. The equation $y'' + y = 0$ is second order.
A solution is a function that makes the equation true. A general solution has arbitrary constants. A particular solution has numbers in place of the constants.
An initial value problem (IVP) is an ODE plus values of the unknown function (and its derivatives) at one starting point. For a first-order ODE:
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(x_0) = y_0 .
The initial condition picks one curve from the family of all solution curves.

Why we solve IVPs. In engineering the starting state is almost always known: the initial charge on a capacitor, the starting temperature of a part, the initial position of a mass. The IVP gives the future behaviour from that start.
Take the IVP $y' = f(x,y)$, $y(x_0)=y_0$. If $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous near the point $(x_0,y_0)$, then the IVP has one and only one solution on some interval around $x_0$.

If the conditions fail, the IVP can have more than one solution. For $y' = 3y^{2/3}$ with $y(0)=0$, both $y=0$ and $y=x^3$ are solutions. Here $\partial f/\partial y = 2y^{-1/3}$ is not continuous at $y=0$.
An equation of the form $\dfrac{\dd y}{\dd x} = g(x)\,h(y)$ is separable.
Move all $y$ terms to one side and all $x$ terms to the other: $\dfrac{\dd y}{h(y)} = g(x)\,\dd x$.
Integrate both sides. Add one constant $C$.
Solve for $y$ if possible. Use the initial condition to find $C$.
Start with $y' = g(x)h(y)$ and assume $h(y)\neq0$. Divide by $h(y)$:
\frac{y'}{h(y)} = g(x).
Let $H(y) = \int \dfrac{\dd y}{h(y)}$, so $H'(y) = 1/h(y)$. By the chain rule,
\frac{\dd}{\dd x}H\big(y(x)\big) = H'(y)\,y' = \frac{y'}{h(y)} = g(x).

Integrate both sides with respect to $x$: $H\big(y(x)\big) = \int g(x)\,\dd x + C$. This is exactly the rule “integrate $\dd y/h(y)$ on the left and $g(x)\,\dd x$ on the right”. Careful: dividing by $h(y)$ loses the constant solutions $y=y_0$ where $h(y_0)=0$. Check them separately.
Solve $\dfrac{\dd y}{\dd x} = 2xy$,   $y(0)=3$.
Separate: $\dfrac{\dd y}{y} = 2x\,\dd x$. Integrate: $\ln|y| = x^2 + C$. So $y = Ae^{x^2}$, where $A = \pm e^{C}$.
Use $y(0)=3$: $3 = Ae^{0} = A$. The solution is
A first-order linear ODE can be written as
Compute the integrating factor $\mu(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,\dd x}$.
Multiply the whole equation by $\mu$. The left side becomes $(\mu y)'$.
Integrate: $\mu y = \int \mu Q\,\dd x + C$.
Divide by $\mu$. Apply the initial condition.
We want a function $\mu(x)$ such that multiplying $y' + Py = Q$ by $\mu$ makes the left side a single derivative. By the product rule,
(\mu y)' = \mu y' + \mu' y .
The left side of $\mu y' + \mu P y = \mu Q$ has this form if $\mu' = P\mu$. This is a separable equation for $\mu$:
\frac{\dd\mu}{\mu} = P\,\dd x \ \Longrightarrow\ \ln\mu = \int P\,\dd x \ \Longrightarrow\ \mu = e^{\int P\,\dd x}.
(We do not need a constant of integration: any one $\mu$ works.) Then the equation reads $(\mu y)' = \mu Q$. Integrate: $\mu y = \int\mu Q\,\dd x + C$, and divide by $\mu$.
Here $P=2$, so $\mu = e^{2x}$. Then $(e^{2x}y)' = 4xe^{2x}$. Integrate by parts:
\int 4xe^{2x}\,\dd x = 2xe^{2x} - e^{2x} + C.
Divide by $e^{2x}$: $y = 2x - 1 + Ce^{-2x}$.
Use $y(0)=1$: $1 = -1 + C$, so $C=2$. The solution is
The equation $M(x,y)\,\dd x + N(x,y)\,\dd y = 0$ is exact if
\frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial N}{\partial x}.
Then there is a function $F(x,y)$ with $F_x = M$ and $F_y = N$, and the solution is $F(x,y) = C$.
Check $M_y = N_x$.
Integrate $M$ with respect to $x$: $F = \int M\,\dd x + g(y)$.
Differentiate $F$ with respect to $y$ and set it equal to $N$. This gives $g'(y)$.
Integrate to find $g(y)$. The solution is $F(x,y)=C$.

blocks.title: The exactness test and the method

blocks.x: Suppose a function $F(x,y)$ exists with $F_x = M$ and $F_y = N$. Along a solution curve $y = y(x)$, the chain rule gives
\frac{\dd}{\dd x}F\big(x,y(x)\big) = F_x + F_y\,y' = M + N\,y' = 0,
because $M\,\dd x + N\,\dd y = 0$ means $M + Ny' = 0$. So $F$ is constant along solutions: $F(x,y)=C$.

Test. If such an $F$ exists, then $M_y = F_{xy}$ and $N_x = F_{yx}$. Mixed partial derivatives of a smooth function are equal, so $M_y = N_x$ is necessary. (On a region without holes it is also sufficient.)
Finding $F$. From $F_x = M$, integrate in $x$. The “constant” of integration may depend on $y$, so $F = \int M\,\dd x + g(y)$. Then $F_y = N$ gives an equation for $g'(y)$, which we integrate.
$M_y = 2x$ and $N_x = 2x$, so the equation is exact. Integrate $M$ with respect to $x$: $F = x^2y + 3x + g(y)$. Then $F_y = x^2 + g'(y)$, which must equal $x^2 + 4y$. So $g' = 4y$ and $g = 2y^2$.
The general solution is $x^2y + 3x + 2y^2 = C$. With $y(1)=1$: $1+3+2 = 6$, so
Integrating factors for non-exact equations
If $M_y \neq N_x$, we can sometimes multiply by a factor $\mu$ to make the equation exact.
If $\dfrac{M_y - N_x}{N}$ depends on $x$ only, use $\mu(x) = \exp\!\Big(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{M_y-N_x}{N}\,\dd x\Big)$.
If $\dfrac{N_x - M_y}{M}$ depends on $y$ only, use $\mu(y) = \exp\!\Big(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{N_x-M_y}{M}\,\dd y\Big)$.
We look for $\mu$ so that $\mu M\,\dd x + \mu N\,\dd y = 0$ is exact: $(\mu M)_y = (\mu N)_x$. Expand with the product rule:
\mu_yM + \mu M_y = \mu_xN + \mu N_x.
If $\mu = \mu(x)$ only, then $\mu_y = 0$ and $\mu_x = \mu'$, so $\mu M_y = \mu'N + \mu N_x$, that is
\frac{\mu'}{\mu} = \frac{M_y - N_x}{N}.
This is solvable (the right side must depend on $x$ only), and $\mu = \exp\int\frac{M_y-N_x}{N}\,\dd x$. If $\mu=\mu(y)$ only, the same steps give $\dfrac{\mu'}{\mu} = \dfrac{N_x - M_y}{M}$.
Solve $(x^2+y^2+x)\,\dd x + xy\,\dd y = 0$.
$M_y = 2y$, $N_x = y$. Not exact. Compute $\dfrac{M_y-N_x}{N} = \dfrac{y}{xy} = \dfrac1x$. So $\mu = e^{\int 1/x\,\dd x} = x$.

Multiply: $(x^3 + xy^2 + x^2)\,\dd x + x^2y\,\dd y = 0$. Now $M_y = 2xy = N_x$. Integrate $M$: $F = \dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{x^2y^2}{2} + \dfrac{x^3}{3} + g(y)$. Then $F_y = x^2y + g'(y) = x^2y$, so $g'=0$. The solution is
The equation $y' + P(x)y = Q(x)y^{n}$ (with $n \neq 0,1$) is a Bernoulli equation.
Substitute $v = y^{1-n}$. Then $v' = (1-n)y^{-n}y'$.
The equation for $v$ is linear: $v' + (1-n)P\,v = (1-n)Q$.
Solve for $v$ with an integrating factor. Then $y = v^{1/(1-n)}$.
Divide $y' + Py = Qy^n$ by $y^n$:
Let $v = y^{1-n}$. Then $v' = (1-n)y^{-n}y'$, so $y^{-n}y' = \dfrac{v'}{1-n}$. Substitute:
\frac{v'}{1-n} + Pv = Q \ \Longrightarrow\ v' + (1-n)P\,v = (1-n)Q .
This is a linear equation for $v$. Solve it with the integrating factor, then return to $y = v^{1/(1-n)}$.
Solve $y' + y = xy^2$.
Here $n=2$. Let $v = y^{-1}$, so $v' = -y^{-2}y'$. Divide the equation by $y^2$: $y^{-2}y' + y^{-1} = x$, which becomes $-v' + v = x$, or

Newton’s law of cooling. The rate of change of temperature $T$ of a body is proportional to the difference between $T$ and the surrounding temperature $T_a$:
\frac{\dd T}{\dd t} = -k\,(T - T_a), \qquad T(0)=T_0 .
The solution is $T = T_a + (T_0 - T_a)e^{-kt}$.
A part at $90^\circ$C is placed in air at $20^\circ$C. After 5 minutes it is at $60^\circ$C. When will it reach $30^\circ$C?
For $T=30$: $10 = 70e^{-kt}$, so $e^{-kt} = \tfrac17$ and $t = \dfrac{\ln 7}{k} = \dfrac{5\ln 7}{\ln(7/4)} \approx 17.4$ minutes.
Figure: cooling curve. The temperature falls fast at first and then slowly approaches $20^\circ$C.
A tank holds 100 litres of pure water. Salt water with $0.5$ kg of salt per litre flows in at 4 L/min. The well-mixed solution flows out at 4 L/min. Find the salt mass $S(t)$ in the tank.
Rate in $= 0.5 \times 4 = 2$ kg/min. Rate out $= \dfrac{S}{100}\times 4 = \dfrac{S}{25}$. So
\frac{\dd S}{\dd t} = 2 - \frac{S}{25}, \qquad S(0)=0.
This is linear and separable. Write $S' + S/25 = 2$, integrating factor $e^{t/25}$: $S = 50 + Ce^{-t/25}$. With $S(0)=0$: $C=-50$, so
As $t\to\infty$, $S\to 50$ kg, which is the concentration $0.5$ kg/L times 100 L.
